title: Exponential Functions, Compound Interest, and e
seo_title: Exponential Growth and Decay Worksheet: Compound Interest and e (Algebra 2) | 100 Questions
standard_text: Construct linear and exponential functions, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, given a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs (include reading these from a table).
meta_desc: Free Algebra 2 worksheet on exponential functions: growth and decay rates, asymptotes, compound interest, continuous growth with e and half-life. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: b > 1: growth. 0 < b < 1: decay. A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt).
key_sub: Continuous growth uses e: A = Pe^(rt).
body_html:
How it works

An exponential function y = a(b)x multiplies by the same factor b each step. If b > 1 it shows growth and if 0 < b < 1 it shows decay. Write b = 1 + r (growth) or 1 − r (decay) to read the percent rate.

y = a(b)x − h + k has the horizontal asymptote y = k.

  • Compound interest: A = P(1 + r/n)nt.
  • Continuous growth: A = Pert, where e ≈ 2.718.
  • Half-life: A = A0(½)t/h.
Example

$2,000 at 6% compounded monthly for 5 years.

2,000(1 + 0.06/12)60

Answer: $2,697.70

Example

$2,000 at 6% compounded continuously for 5 years.

2,000e0.3

Answer: $2,699.72

Common mistakes

  • Reading the rate from the base: b = 0.85 is a 15% decay, not 85%.
  • Forgetting to divide the rate by n or to multiply the time by n.
  • Using 6 instead of 0.06 for 6%.
  • Thinking the graph crosses its asymptote. It gets close but never reaches it.

faq.q: How can you tell if an exponential function shows growth or decay?
faq.a: Look at the base b. If b is greater than 1 it is growth; if b is between 0 and 1 it is decay.

faq.q: What is the compound interest formula?
faq.a: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where P is the principal, r is the annual rate as a decimal, n is the number of compounding periods per year and t is the time in years.
e ≈ 2.71828 is the base for continuous growth. Money compounded continuously grows as A = Pe^(rt).
The time it takes for a quantity to fall to half its amount. After n half-lives, (1/2)^n of the original amount is left.
